title: The Pre-Sale That Worked and the Payment Bas van Abel Feared to Send
dek: In 2013 Fairphone asked 5,000 people to pay in advance for a phone that did not yet exist, and its founder then hesitated over the order.

story.event: Pre-selling 5,000 phones to pay for the first production run
story.summary: In May 2013 Fairphone, a new Amsterdam social enterprise that grew out of a 2010 campaign on conflict minerals, began pre-selling a €325 phone and needed 5,000 paid orders to place its first production order in China without outside investors. It passed the target in early June. Bas van Abel later said he nearly returned the money instead of transferring €1.5 million to the manufacturer; about 25,000 phones were sold in 2013.
paragraphs: Fairphone began in 2010 as a campaign, not a company. Bas van Abel, a designer who ran the Open Design Lab at Amsterdam's Waag Society, was asked by a friend at ActionAid to help with a campaign about conflict minerals: the tin, tantalum, tungsten and gold whose trade had helped pay for war in eastern Congo. To make people look at what was inside their phones, the team decided to make one. "We said, 'If we sell 5,000 of these phones, we'd do it,'" he later recalled.

In May 2013 the newly formed social enterprise, eight people at the time, began taking pre-orders on its own website: €325 for an Android phone nobody could yet hold. Five thousand paid orders would let it place a purchase order with its Chinese suppliers without outside investors. The start was slow. Sales went first to the more than 16,000 people who had registered interest, and on 24 May, with 20 days left, TechCrunch counted 2,333 phones sold. The pre-sale was opened to anyone in Europe.

The target fell in the first days of June, about three weeks after sales opened and with more than a week to spare. Van Abel said buyers had paid for a phone "they haven't held in their own hands." Then came the order itself. Two years later he told Tech.eu that when he had to transfer €1.5 million to the manufacturer he panicked: "I couldn't push the damn button on my laptop." Perhaps, he thought, they should stop there, return everyone's money and call it a day, since the point had been made. He made the payment.

About 25,000 Fairphones were sold in 2013. They were not perfectly fair, and he said so: the tin and tantalum came from conflict-free mines, but conditions in Congolese mines and Chinese factories were far from ideal. "We should get criticized," he told NPR in 2014. "This is work in progress."

quote.text: From these definitions it follows, that there is no hope unmingled with fear, and no fear unmingled with hope.
quote.locator: Part III, Definitions of the Emotions, XIII, Explanation
quote.source_title: Ethics, tr. R. H. M. Elwes, Project Gutenberg eBook #3800
quote.connection: Van Abel's panic came at the moment of success, not failure. Spinoza suggests why that is less strange than it feels: hope and fear grow from the same uncertainty, so the more people had trusted him with, the more there was to be afraid of losing.

reflection: It is unsettling when the hardest moment arrives after the good news. The orders had come in; the doubt came with the money. That did not mean the plan was wrong. It meant something real was now at stake, other people's trust as well as his own.

When you next feel a jolt of fear at a yes you asked for, whether from a client, a colleague offering help or your family agreeing to a plan, it may help to read the fear as a measure of the hope rather than a verdict on it. Then decide the next step on its merits, ideally after a night's sleep.
invitation: Think of one commitment you have been circling because it now feels real. Write down the single next action it needs and the day you will take it. That is enough for this morning.

cross_checks.claim: Fairphone needed 5,000 paid pre-orders at €325 to start production
The 5,000 target was reached in early June 2013, about three weeks after sales opened and more than a week before the campaign closed
Fairphone began as a 2010 campaign on conflict minerals with ActionAid and Waag
Pre-sales let Fairphone fund production without outside investors
About 25,000 Fairphones were sold in 2013, the first wave

research_notes: Pre-order pace: the contemporary record (Waag's release and Fairphone's own blog in 2013, TechCrunch on 24 May with 2,333 sold, The Register on 5 June) shows the 5,000 target reached about three weeks after sales opened; NPR (2014) and Tech.eu (2015) say 10,000 orders came in within three weeks. The story uses the contemporary figure. Exact day: The Register (5 June) says the target was reached 'today', Engadget (5 June, not cited) says 'yesterday', and Fairphone's blog says nine days were left before 14 June while The Register says orders stayed open until 13 June; the story says 'the first days of June' and 'more than a week to spare'. Waag's page carries a 21 May 2013 publication date in its metadata that cannot be right for a release announcing the 5,000 milestone, so no date is taken from it. Production: Waag and The Register give a first run of 20,000; NPR and The Big Issue say about 25,000 were sold in 2013; the story gives the sales figure only. Team size: eight people in Waag's 2013 release; van Abel later told The Big Issue the team was 'five people who didn't know how to make phones'; the story uses the contemporary eight. The €1.5 million transfer and the button remark come only from van Abel's 2015 interview with Tech.eu and are attributed to him; Tech.eu places the moment after the campaign, when 'several million euros' had come in, so the story does not date it to the day the target was reached. NPR's $3.5 million within a month is not used. Van Abel has also said (Fairphone podcast, The Big Issue) that early work in Congo involved paying bribes; that is outside this episode and is not included. Funding is 'bootstrapped' in the sense that the first production run was paid for by customers' advance payments rather than investors; the project itself emerged from a nonprofit lab's research programme. The Spinoza line is a definition in his account of the emotions; it is applied by analogy.
